narrative:
Based on the assessment, there is a 20% chance you will fail your final year. While this may not seem high, it exceeds the 10% threshold that triggers the requirement for remedial courses — a precautionary measure designed to support students before difficulties become serious.

The three factors that most shaped this prediction actually all worked in your favour, which is encouraging. The most influential factor was your clean academic record: you have no past class failures, matching perfectly the average among students who are not required to take remedial courses. This is a strong positive signal. The second most influential factor was your weekend alcohol consumption, which you report as very low — notably better than many peers, where medium or higher consumption is common. This also pushed your prediction toward passing. Third, your clear ambition to pursue higher education — a goal shared by every student in the comparison group — further reduced your predicted risk of failing.

So why are you still required to take remedial courses? Because despite these positive factors, other aspects of your profile — such as your 9 school absences compared to an average of just 2.8 among passing students, and your high levels of free time and going out with friends — collectively raised enough concern to push the overall risk above the threshold.

The remedial courses are not a punishment; they are a safety net. You should attend them consistently, work on reducing absences, and consider whether your current balance between social activities and study time is setting you up for the success you clearly want.
